title: Henry II to Suleiman, 1547: Malvezzi's enciphered Latin copy of d'Huyson's credence and two other letters (catalogue 500, HHStA Türkei I 7-2-18)

steps.what: Malvezzi alphabet (R367/R386) calibrated on 7-3-20 f. 44 with its contemporary decipherment (f. 45); frozen as K-C01.
Blind validation of the frozen alphabet (8-3-8).
Sign-by-sign re-reading of all lines in four passes (C12-C15) on the native images.
About 97.5% of groups read; Latin text of three letters of Henry II and Malvezzi's Italian notes, with English translation; captain Bartolomeo identified from Morvilliers (Charrière II).

texts.label: Henry II to Suleiman (credence for d'Huyson and two other letters), Malvezzi's enciphered copy, HHStA Türkei I 7-2-18
texts.summary: In the autumn of 1547 Henry II, king for six months, sent his pantler, the sieur d’Huyson, to Constantinople with a letter of credence for Suleiman and instructions: join the truce that Charles V and Ferdinand had just made with the Porte, but have the king’s allies — the Swiss first — included in it, and expose imperial bad faith. Ferdinand’s resident in Constantinople, Giovanni Maria Malvezzi, got hold of the text, translated it back “from Turkish into Latin, word for word” and sent it to Vienna in cipher, together with a second, longer letter and a third, carried by a captain, about the Diet of Augsburg and asking for the Ottoman fleet. No earlier decipherment of the cipher is known; the archive's catalogue marks it not deciphered.

reading_review.note: Read reading.md (Latin and Italian) against translation.md section by section: the credence, Malvezzi's note, the long letter and the third letter build coherent sentences throughout, with 27 scattered ‹…› holes and 86 probable readings in braces; the weakest passages are the Italian heading (143r ll. 1-2), the three groups after 'ne deceptione' (143v l. 30) and 'imo ‹…› cum ‹…›'. The Latin is a back-translation from Turkish, so its syntax wavers between persons.
